sections.html: Discus are among the most stunning of all aquarium fish and remain a beautiful addition to any large show aquarium. They were first introduced to aquarists in 1933 and were made internationally popular by Dr. Herbert R. Axelrod. Fully grown, an adult can reach about 15 cm (6 inches). They are regarded as one of the most challenging freshwater tropical fish to keep.

Like the Angelfish (Pterophyllum) and Cichlasoma festivum, the Discus inhabits the vast Amazon region, extending from the middle reaches of the Amazon River far into the jungles of the Venezuelan and Peruvian flood basins.

The Discus is quite commonly found among profuse plant growth in the quiet bends of rivers, under overhanging banks, and among rock crannies. In shallow areas, it cares for its young beneath the leaves of various Nymphaea species.

The absolute minimum aquarium size for young Discus is 100 × 50 × 50 cm (40 × 20 × 20 inches). Adult Discus need an aquarium 150 cm (5 feet) long, or about 285 litres (75 gallons) minimum, to be happy and have any chance of breeding successfully. Breeding can happen in a smaller aquarium, but for maximum success 285 litres minimum, well planted and well filtered, is suggested. Discus do not like changes in water conditions, and the larger the body of water, the more gradual those changes are.

The Discus needs very pure, clean water filtered through peat, in a well-established planted aquarium. Temperature should be a steady 28°C (82°F), pH 6.5–7.5, 1–12 dGH.

For breeding: 30°C (86°F), pH 6–6.5, 0–5 dGH.

The Discus is a finicky eater. It is very important to give a diet of live and frozen food. On a diet of dry flake food they will quickly die, though it may be offered occasionally as a supplement. When rearing fry, the fry feed off the parents' sides, so both the male and the female need extra protein.

Very peaceful; it does not burrow in the substrate like many cichlids and does not dig up or tear up plants. The Discus lives in harmony with other fish, except at spawning time, when it vigorously defends its young.

It is best to get a group of young Discus and let them pair off; a Discus mates for life. It is obvious when mates have found each other: they no longer stay with the group but stake out their own portion of the aquarium as a territory. Only one pair should be left in any one aquarium if successful breeding is wanted. The rest of the young can be moved to another aquarium, where another pair may find each other.

Can be sexed only by experts. At spawning time the genital papilla is pointed in males and flat and round in females. Viewed from above at breeding time, females are slightly fatter due to being filled with roe (eggs).

For the first 4 days or so the parents move the fry from one place to another in the aquarium, much like angelfish. When the fry become free swimming, they go immediately to the parent's sides. At first it looks like they are clinging for protection, but they are in fact eating something from under the parent's scales. The fry dig their heads in under a scale and jerk from side to side, breaking off "food". Eventually one parent tires of the constant pecking and shakes the fry off, and the fry go immediately to the other parent and do the same. This goes back and forth for weeks, until the young are mature enough for life on their own among the plants in the aquarium.

Viewed from the front, Discus are extremely thin for their size, but from the side they are nearly round, hence the name discus, Latin for plate or dish. Their basic body colour in nature is brown. Brilliant blue bars cover both the dorsal and anal fins and extend onto the back and belly. The dorsal, ventral and anal fins are edged in bright red.

A variety from Lake Tefé, Brazil, has bright metallic green or blue bars all over its fins and body and is occasionally called the Royal Discus.

Over the decades many varieties have appeared, such as red, yellow, and orange to yellow forms like the Sunset Discus. These varieties do not occur in nature; they have been developed over many years of careful breeding.
